passage: Road safety is a shared responsibility that relies on understanding physics and strict adherence to traffic regulations. When approaching a traffic signal, a yellow light serves as a warning to slow down and prepare to stop, not an invitation to accelerate. Road signs are categorized by shape; for instance, circular signs indicate mandatory orders that must be followed, while triangular signs warn of hazards. Safety equipment is non-negotiable for all occupants. Every passenger in a vehicle, whether in the front or back seat, must wear a seatbelt, and children should always be secured in appropriate child restraints rather than sitting on an adult's lap. Similarly, on a two-wheeler, both the rider and the pillion passenger must wear a securely fastened helmet, regardless of the distance traveled. Physics dictates that speed is a critical factor in crash severity; doubling your speed increases the kinetic energy fourfold, making a collision significantly more dangerous than just twice as bad. Furthermore, driving under the influence of alcohol is never safe, as it impairs reaction times and judgment, regardless of how relaxed a driver feels. Finally, if you are walking on a road without a footpath, always walk facing the oncoming traffic so you can see vehicles approaching you. These rules exist to protect lives, not merely to facilitate law enforcement.

items.evidence: When approaching a traffic signal, a yellow light serves as a warning to slow down and prepare to stop, not an invitation to accelerate.
items.q: Meera is driving towards a signal when it turns yellow. What should she do?
options: Slow down and get ready to stop
Speed up to cross before it turns red
Keep going at the same speed, like green
Keep going unless a policeman is watching
items.explain: A yellow light is a warning to slow down and prepare to stop, not to speed up.

wrong.why: thinks yellow means hurry through before red
thinks amber means the same as green
thinks traffic rules are only advice

items.evidence: Road signs are categorized by shape; for instance, circular signs indicate mandatory orders that must be followed, while triangular signs warn of hazards.
items.q: A driver sees a round road sign ahead. How should the driver treat it?
options: As a rule that has to be obeyed
As a warning about a danger ahead
As helpful advice that can be ignored
As meaning only what its picture shows
items.explain: Circular signs give orders that must be followed; triangular signs are the ones that warn of hazards.

wrong.why: mixes up circular signs with triangular warning signs
thinks the shape of a sign does not matter

items.evidence: Every passenger in a vehicle, whether in the front or back seat, must wear a seatbelt, and children should always be secured in appropriate child restraints rather than sitting on an adult's lap.
items.q: Four friends ride in a car, two in front and two behind. Who must wear seatbelts?
options: Everyone sitting in the front and back
Only the driver and the front passenger
Nobody, as long as the car goes slowly
Only the people sitting without an airbag
items.explain: Every passenger, in the front or back seat, must wear a seatbelt.

wrong.why: thinks only front-seat passengers need belts
thinks belts are not needed at low speed
thinks an airbag replaces the seatbelt

items.evidence: Similarly, on a two-wheeler, both the rider and the pillion passenger must wear a securely fastened helmet, regardless of the distance traveled.
items.q: Aman takes his sister on his scooter for a short ride to the market. Who needs a helmet?
options: Both of them, with straps fastened tightly
Only Aman, since he is the rider
Neither of them, since the trip is short
Both of them, but straps can stay loose
items.explain: Rider and pillion must both wear securely fastened helmets, however short the trip.

wrong.why: thinks only the rider needs a helmet
thinks helmets are only for long trips
thinks a loose helmet still protects

items.evidence: Physics dictates that speed is a critical factor in crash severity; doubling your speed increases the kinetic energy fourfold, making a collision significantly more dangerous than just twice as bad.
items.q: A car speeds up from 30 km/h to 60 km/h. How does its energy in a crash change?
options: It becomes four times as large
It becomes two times as large
It stays about the same as before
It becomes a little bit larger
items.explain: Doubling speed makes kinetic energy four times larger, so the crash is far worse than twice as bad.

wrong.why: thinks energy grows in step with speed
thinks speed does not affect crash severity
